name: Tharti-Tharti / Dadidadi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Blake, Barry J., Luise Hercus, Stephen Morey & Edward Ryan. 2011. The Mathi group of languages. Pacific Linguistics 628. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, The Australian National University. (Open Access, ANU Open Research handle 1885/17910.) Corroboration: Hercus, Luise A. 1986. Victorian languages: a late survey. catalog_locator: sec. 3.1.8 'The Mathi-Mathi accentuation system from a wider perspective', p. 76; corroboration Hercus 1986 p. 232
catalog_quote: The evidence that there was indeed such an areal feature is by no means obvious. If we start among the River languages closest to Mathi-Mathi there is no evidence for accents in Yitha-Yitha, and Keramin. Every one of the few Tharti-Tharti words recorded by Jack Long was accented on the first syllable There are only a few words in Yitha-Yitha, Tharti-Tharti and Keramin that have initial clusters that might have arisen from loss of a vowel in the initial syllable such as troot ‘knee’ noted by Beveridge and recorded as trut by Jack Long for Tharti-Tharti: in these cases it is quite likely that the initial clusters could have arisen through metathesis (*turt > trut).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the only modern phonetic record of the language (a few dozen Tharti-Tharti = Dadi Dadi words remembered by Jack Long and recorded by Hercus), every word carried the accent on the first syllable; the 19th-century Yitha-Yitha sources mark no accent at all, and the authors reject the idea of a Murray-River second-syllable stress shift for these varieties. Corroborated by Hercus 1986:232, where all c. 30 Dadidadi vocabulary items are transcribed with initial primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated; Hercus 1986:232 marks a secondary stress on the second syllable of one item, nanar ['naˌna·r] 'man'.
new_statements.exceptions: None; initial clusters (trut 'knee') explained as metathesis rather than loss of an unstressed first vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation-form words from a rememberer (not a fluent speaker); corpus of a few dozen words; statement is an observation over that corpus, not a phonological rule from a grammar of the language.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog lowe1403 is a language-level node with two dialects, Yitha Yitha (yith1234, lower Lachlan) and Dadi Dadi / Tharti-Tharti / Dadidadi (dadi1251, Murray around Euston); Hercus 1986:101, 232 calls the two 'almost, or perhaps completely, identical'. The quoted statement (Blake et al. 2011:76) and the stress-marked vocabulary (Hercus 1986:232) concern Tharti-Tharti = Dadi Dadi (dadi1251) specifically: a few dozen words remembered by Jack Long (a Mathi-Mathi speaker whose mother was part Dadidadi), recorded by Hercus in the 1960s-70s. For Yitha Yitha proper the same source says the old records carry no accent marking ('no evidence for accents in Yitha-Yitha').

sources.note: p.76: in arguing against Goedemans' 'areal stress shift along the Murray', states there is no evidence for accents in Yitha-Yitha and Keramin (old sources unmarked), and 'Every one of the few Tharti-Tharti words recorded by Jack Long was accented on the first syllable'; initial clusters like trut 'knee' attributed to metathesis, not first-vowel loss.

sources.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1986. Victorian languages: a late survey. Pacific Linguistics B-77. Canberra: ANU. (sec. 4.1 p.101; 'A note on Narinari' pp.152-155; Dadidadi vocabulary p.232)
sources.note: No rule statement for Dadidadi/Yidayida; p.232 'Dadidadi vocabulary' (c. 30 items from Jack Long) transcribes every word with primary stress on the first syllable (['barʌk] kangaroo, ['bikUrU] kangaroo, ['θarkUkI] bread, ['diŋgata] to sit, ['rinmə] child, ['wɔkwoi] possum; nanar ['naˌna·r] man with secondary on 2nd). p.231: phonemic system for Dadidadi 'must be regarded as hypothetical, because of the shortage of material'. p.101, 152: the languages are extinct; other sources are Curr, Smyth, Cameron, Larmer wordlists and an R.H. Mathews MS sketch.
